1. Introduction & Data

This report analyzes 1,004,894 crime incidents recorded by the Los Angeles Police Department between 2020-01-01 and 2024-12-30, covering all 21 LAPD geographic areas and 140 distinct crime categories. The raw file contained 27 fields per record (dates, times, location, victim demographics, weapon, premise, and case status); this analysis focuses on the subset most relevant to understanding when, where, what kind, and to whom crime occurred, and how effectively cases were resolved.

Data quality note. Victim age values of 0 or below were treated as missing (crimes such as vehicle theft have no personal victim). Victim sex codes outside M/F were bucketed as "Unknown." All timestamps were parsed from the LAPD's native MM/DD/YYYY and HHMM formats. No rows fell outside the stated 2020–2024 window.

2. Time Trends

Crime volume was essentially flat through 2020–2021, climbed steadily through 2022, and stayed high through 2023 before an apparent sharp drop in 2024.

Important caveat on the 2024 "drop." The steep decline visible from roughly April 2024 onward is not a real fall in crime — it is a data-completeness artifact. Incident counts decline in an almost perfectly smooth, monotonic staircase from 232,345 in 2023 to 127,567 in 2024, with December 2024 showing only 4697 incidents versus ~19,500–20,000/month in the same dataset's 2023 figures. This pattern is the signature of a dataset extract taken partway through processing: recent months hadn't yet had all their incident reports entered/finalized at the time this file was pulled. Any year-over-year comparison involving 2024 should be treated with caution — it understates true 2024 volume, likely substantially.

3. Crime Types

Vehicle theft is the single largest category, driven partly by the fact that it's a well-defined, always-reported crime (owners need a police report for insurance). The top 15 categories account for a large share of total volume, but the long tail of 140 total crime types shows how varied LA's crime landscape is.

4. Geography

The Central area recorded the most incidents (69,668), nearly double the lowest-volume area, Foothill (33,129). This partly reflects Central's dense commercial/downtown footprint, which draws more foot traffic, retail, and transient population than residential-heavy areas like Foothill.

5. Victim Demographics

Among incidents with a personal victim and recorded age, the median victim age is 37 (mean 39.5). Sex is recorded as male in 40.2% of records, female in 35.7%, with 24.1% unknown/not applicable (reflecting crimes without a personal victim, like vehicle theft).

6. Weapons & Premises

A weapon or force type is recorded in 32.6% of incidents. Of those, the large majority involve no weapon in the traditional sense — "strong-arm" (hands/fists/feet) dominates, consistent with simple assault being one of the most common crime types.

7. Case Resolution

Only 9.0% of all cases in this dataset resulted in an arrest (adult or juvenile). The overwhelming majority (79.9%) remain marked "Investigation Continued." This is a fairly typical clearance rate for a large urban department across all crime types combined, but it varies enormously by crime type.

9. Can We Predict Whether a Case Gets an Arrest?

Section 7 showed clearance rates vary a lot by crime type. To understand that variation more rigorously, this section trains two classifiers — Logistic Regression and Random Forest — to predict, from case characteristics alone (crime type, weapon, premise, area, victim sex/age, hour, day of week), whether a case will result in an arrest. Both models were trained on 927,247 incidents (the 30 most common crime types) with a 75/25 train/test split, against a base arrest rate of 8.5%.

What this model tells us. An AUC around 0.79 means the model can meaningfully rank "more likely to be cleared" vs. "less likely" cases, but it's far from a crystal ball — there's a lot of case-specific variation (witness cooperation, evidence quality, officer follow-up) this dataset simply doesn't capture. The practical takeaway is less about prediction and more about diagnosis: what type of crime occurred and whether a weapon was involved explain the large majority of variation in clearance, far more than where or when it happened.

10. Key Takeaways

  1. Crime rose through 2022 then plateaued — the apparent 2024 crash is a reporting-lag artifact in this specific data extract, not a real decline.
  2. Vehicle-related crime dominates — stolen vehicles, burglary from vehicle, and theft from vehicle together account for a large share of all incidents, and cluster in the evening/overnight hours.
  3. Friday evenings are the highest-risk window citywide, consistent across most crime types.
  4. Central division sees the most crime, roughly double the lowest-volume area, driven by its dense, mixed commercial footprint.
  5. Clearance rates are low overall (9%) and highly uneven — violent interpersonal crime clears at 20%+ while anonymous property crime rarely does.
  6. Two data-quality patterns are worth flagging to anyone building on this dataset: the 2024 volume drop-off, and midnight/noon timestamp clustering in identity theft (and likely other delayed-discovery crimes).
  7. Crime concentrates geographically — DBSCAN finds ~37% of incidents fall inside one of just 451 dense micro-hotspots, several of them downtown around Central/Olympic/Rampart.
  8. Arrest outcomes are predictable mainly from crime type and weapon (AUC ~0.79), not from when or where the crime happened — location and time matter far less than what kind of crime it was.
